mappings.note: The procedure for infusing cloth strips with chopped onion to make an olfactory indicator is preparing apparatus for an investigation. Not LO-15, because the method is prescribed, not designed by the student.
Blue hydrangea flowers are related back to acidic soil, a phenomenon tied to its cause. Not LO-4, because nothing is tested; the plant colour is read as evidence about the soil.
The basic-soil companion of the hydrangea item, same phenomenon-and-cause reasoning in the opposite direction.

P.C. Ray as Father of Modern Indian Chemistry and founder of the first Indian pharmaceutical company is a story of scientific achievement. Not LO-16, since no value of honesty or objectivity is in question.
Also from the P.C. Ray biography box, this time his advocacy of the mother tongue. Still the discuss-and-appreciate-the-scientist outcome; nothing chemical is assessed.
Names neutralisation as the process when acid and base are mixed. Not LO-7, because no word equation is written; only the process is named.

Salt and water as the products is the acid plus base gives salt plus water word equation that LO-7 names for acid-base reactions. Chosen over LO-6, which would cover explaining why neutralisation happens rather than reciting its products.
Tracks the litmus colour back to blue as lime water is added, i.e. explaining the neutralisation process as it proceeds. Not LO-7, since the products are never named.
Reads the observed heat as evidence that the reaction is exothermic: an observation related to what causes it. Not LO-6, because the process itself is taken as given and only the heat is interpreted.
Baking soda on an ant sting is the classic dealing-with-acidity application named in LO-13. Not LO-6, because the neutralisation is the means and the everyday remedy is the point.

Naming formic acid as what an ant injects is recall of a substance in a familiar context. Kept at competency level for the same reason as the citric and ascorbic acid items: no outcome covers naming the acid in a material.
A farmer liming over-acidic soil is treating soil, named verbatim in LO-13. Not LO-14, because the aim is crop growth, not reducing a pollutant.
Organic matter for over-basic soil is the same soil-treatment application in the opposite direction.

Contrasts the two soil treatments. It stays with the two single-treatment items on LO-13 because the frame has only one outcome for soil correction; the contrast is between remedies, not between materials, so LO-2 does not apply.

Neutralising acidic factory effluent before it reaches a lake is minimising a pollutant to protect aquatic life, which is LO-14. Chosen over LO-13 because the beneficiary is the environment, not the person applying the remedy.

Requires knowing which of four familiar cases actually is a neutralisation and that dissolving chuna is not, i.e. a grip on the process. Not LO-13, because the test is conceptual even though the options are applications.

Why the sprayed turmeric makes soap-solution writing appear: the visible effect is traced to the base reacting with the indicator. Not LO-15, because the design is given and only the cause is asked for.

The assertion is the product list salt, water and heat and the reason is the acid-base reaction, so the item rests on the neutralisation word equation. Not LO-6, since the products rather than the process carry the marks.
Identifies red rose extract from its red-in-acid, green-in-base behaviour, i.e. knowledge of the indicator itself. Not LO-3, because no substance is being classified.
Assigns a single solution to the basic class from one litmus result. Not LO-2, which in this chapter covers items where two or more substances must be told apart.
Four candidate substances, only one acidic, must be told apart to reverse a basic solution. That sorting is LO-2, not LO-3, because the work is in discriminating the options.
Three solutions and three different indicators must be resolved together, a multi-substance differentiation. Not LO-4, since the results are supplied rather than obtained.
One green red-rose strip, one solution to place in the basic class. Single-substance classification, so LO-3 rather than LO-2.
One liquid, three indicator results, one class to assign: acidic. Again classification of a single sample rather than discrimination between samples.
Choosing an olfactory indicator for a blindfolded tester is selecting a workable test method, the planning side of LO-4. Not LO-2, since no substance is identified in the item.

Grape juice is inferred to be acidic and the student must say what a base then does to it, which is explaining the neutralisation and the resulting colour shift. Not LO-5, because a process is followed through rather than a single effect traced to a cause.
Picking the method that reveals acidic invisible writing is choosing the right test. Not LO-13, because revealing a secret message is a classroom exercise, not a day-to-day acidity problem.
Extraction by water or paste as the way to prepare turmeric and red rose indicators: the coloured-extract indicator investigation of LO-4.

Turmeric cannot separate an acid from a neutral solution, so the item tests whether a chosen indicator is adequate for the query. That is the investigation-planning outcome, not a classification of the three liquids.
Liquid X is basic and excess amla juice drives it acidic; the marks turn on following the neutralisation through to the indicator colour. The class of X is a preliminary step, so LO-3 is not cited.
Reads the two branches of the unhealthy-plant flow chart. Anchored to the flow chart itself, so LO-9 rather than LO-13, which covers the soil remedies the chart then leads to.
Lime as the treatment for acidic soil, the soil-treatment application named in LO-13.

Bubbling on eggshell with vinegar but not with soap is traced to acid reacting with carbonate to release carbon dioxide: a phenomenon related to its cause. Not LO-6, since neutralisation is not what is happening here and no process is described step by step.

Which exploratory activities the chapter proposes, indicator rangoli and testing water and soil samples, is about what can be investigated with natural indicators. Not LO-15, because the student recalls the suggested projects rather than designing one.
Recall of the blue-litmus-to-red result. Grouped with the other indicator-result items on LO-4: the observation belongs to the indicator test, and no substance is being classified here.
Recall of the red-litmus-to-blue result, the companion observation to the previous item and the same outcome for the same reason.
Defines acid-base indicator; the vocabulary of the indicator investigation.

Naming the fungus and alga that make up a lichen is identifying organisms. Kept at the competency because LO-1 keys on observable features such as appearance and texture, and the partnership inside a lichen is not observed by the student.
Sour as the general taste of acids is identification by an observable feature. Not LO-3, since no class boundary is being drawn, only a property stated.
Citric acid in lemon; same competency-level placement as the other name-the-acid items in this chapter.
